question: When a multi-head Transformer must copy several groups of past positions with unequal statistical importance, why do all heads first compete for the dominant sparse pattern and only later cooperate by specializing, and which parts of that staged trajectory can be proved?

key_findings.claim: Author contribution: a high-order Markov task makes multiple position-copying patterns necessary while ordering their statistical importance, and a one-layer multi-head attention model can represent the target with one sparse head per group.
key_findings.evidence: The next-token logits sum h feature maps A-star-k applied to weighted, disjoint lag groups I(k), ordered by matrix norm. The constructive solution uses one-hot positional coordinates, attention mass alpha-i on the appropriate lags, and value matrix [A-star-k, 0]. Exact sparsity is a limiting logit-separation statement rather than a finite-parameter property. Appendix A also proves the data-generating distribution is non-identifiable: overlapping, nonsparse head decompositions can express the same logits.

anchors.section: 2.2 Representing the Task with Sparse Attention

key_findings.claim: Author-reported central phenomenon: three-head Transformers first place overlapping attention on the most important lag group and then specialize one head at a time on less important groups.
key_findings.evidence: In the default h=3, w=12 experiment, attention is uniform at initialization, all three heads overlap mainly on I(1) by step 60, one head moves to I(2) by step 300, and the three patterns are separated by step 1000. The value matrices evolve jointly: a non-offshooting ensemble compensates for cross-terms from the head leaving the dominant pattern. This supports a competitive-to-cooperative description, but it is a small synthetic model and the plotted run is not accompanied by seed uncertainty.

anchors.section: D.1 Numerical Simulations of the Regression Flow

key_findings.claim: Author-reported functional result: the stages are not merely attention visualizations; the full model successively approaches predictors that use progressively longer effective contexts.
key_findings.evidence: The full-context model is compared with restricted-context Transformers at c=4, 8, and 12 and with ground-truth predictors using I(1), I(1) union I(2), and all three groups. Intermediate KL curves dip and rise as the full model passes their neighborhoods, while divergence to the complete predictor stays low only after the final stage. This demonstrates a sequence of misspecified effective models on this task, not a universal hierarchy for language.

anchors.section: Figure 3 stage-wise learning in function space

key_findings.claim: Author-reported negative results: exact head symmetry prevents specialization, and removing the feature-importance ordering collapses three acquisition stages into two.
key_findings.evidence: With attention initialization scale u=0, heads remain exactly symmetric and learn only one pattern; smaller nonzero u slows symmetry breaking. With equal feature norms m=1, one pattern is acquired first through random symmetry breaking and the other two arrive together, whereas m=1.3 and 1.5 produce three increasingly distinct stages. These results make perturbation and importance gaps necessary ingredients of the observed default trajectory.

anchors.section: Appendix C expansion around near-uniform initialization

key_findings.claim: Author-reported data-size result with reviewer qualification: fewer training examples truncate the stage sequence, and early stopping selects a shorter effective context, but the claimed sample-complexity benefit is not directly measured.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 5 reports fewer stage transitions as dataset size falls; at 600 samples the model emphasizes the first two patterns and gives little weight to the third even while feature matrices overfit. Restricted-context KL comparisons support an effective-context interpretation. The paper connects this to implicit regularization and possible sample efficiency, but supplies neither a formal generalization bound for this Transformer nor a quantitative comparison showing that the truncated trajectory improves held-out risk over competing regularizers.

Related work on data-dependent stage progression

key_findings.claim: Author theorem: under isotropic inputs, zero-mean noise, orthogonal feature matrices, singleton lag groups, and population gradient flow, the regression surrogate becomes a nonlinear tensor-factorization flow.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 1 rewrites the population mean-squared loss as one half the squared Frobenius distance between G=sum m-star-k V-star-k tensor s-star-k and P=sum V-k tensor s-k. The attention variables evolve through the softmax-simplex projection Pi(s). The reduction is exact under the stated surrogate assumptions, which deliberately remove finite-sample cross-entropy, general covariance, and nonsingleton groups.

key_findings.claim: Author theorem: in the idealized competitive phase, coupled heads converge to the dominant position-feature pair, while near-coupled heads remain close only for a controlled finite time.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 1 proves that ordered alignment with the first feature yields V(infinity)=m-star-1 V-star-1/h and s(infinity)=s-star-1. Theorem 2 bounds deviations from the symmetric system by epsilon exp(c t) up to a time proportional to negative log epsilon. The proof uses a forward-invariant ordering region and a monotone Lyapunov potential. Thus the result explains attraction toward the first saddle, not global convergence of arbitrary randomly initialized full Transformers.

anchors.section: 3.2 Coupled Dynamics Describe the Competitive Phase / Theorems 1-2

key_findings.claim: Author theorem and empirical bridge: after the dominant saddle, a perturbed head can offshoot toward the next feature while the remaining heads compensate, and the simplified flow tracks the simulated regression dynamics.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3 supplies another finite-time closeness bound for an offshooting head plus coupled ensemble, conditional on staying delta away from the first attention vertex. Lemma 1 motivates a fast-ensemble approximation; Theorem 4 then proves convergence of the free head to m-star-2 V-star-2 and s-star-2 under ordered alignment and a positive-potential condition. In Figure 7, simplified ODEs initialized at t=25 and t=300 track attention and value trajectories, including nonmonotonic compensatory dips; Figures 6 and 8 show the same qualitative signature in regression and classification settings.

anchors.section: 3.3 Cooperation After Competition / Theorem 3 and Lemma 1

key_findings.claim: Author-reported robustness and negative audit: the staged pattern survives several controlled variations, while weight decay produces almost no observable change and ambiguous overlap can select different sparse solutions.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix F reproduces stage-wise behavior under online infinite data, reversed importance order, two-block minimal and full Transformers, nonuniform within-group weights, overlapping intervals with three or four heads, and SGD. The authors report almost no difference without weight decay and omit its plot. In the overlapping setting, statistical importance is unclear and different head counts follow different solutions, consistent with the task's non-identifiability rather than a unique recovery theorem.

anchors.section: F.3-F.6 weight decay, depth, nonuniform weights, and overlap

key_findings.claim: Contradiction audit: the arbitrary-stage theorem appears to drop the target feature magnitude in its stated limit.
key_findings.evidence: Section 3.1 defines V-star-k as the unit-Frobenius feature direction and G with coefficient m-star-k. Theorem 4 correspondingly concludes V-prime(infinity)=m-star-2 V-star-2. Appendix Theorem 5 instead states V-n(infinity)=V-star-n without m-star-n, even though its residual target G^(n-1) retains those coefficients and the proof is said to follow Theorem 4 mutatis mutandis. Unless an unstated renormalization occurs, this is a scale inconsistency or typographical omission, so the higher-order theorem should be checked against the source derivation.

anchors.section: 3.1 definitions of m-star-k, V-star-k, and G

key_findings.claim: Reviewer inference: the defensible novelty is a head-interaction mechanism for a controlled multi-pattern copying task, not a general explanation of specialization or emergence in language models.
key_findings.evidence: Prior work already studies stage-wise n-gram learning, sparse-attention emergence, induction-head training, and multi-head task allocation. This paper's narrower addition is the competitive phase in which symmetric heads initially learn the same dominant positional pattern, followed by sequential offshooting and value-matrix compensation, with a matched tensor-factorization surrogate. The empirical evidence remains one synthetic process family, small one- and two-block models, predominantly single plotted runs, and qualitative transfer between regression theory and classification experiments.

method.core_idea: Use an importance-ordered high-order Markov process to expose how symmetric attention heads coordinate while learning several sparse copying rules, then model the observed competition, offshooting, and compensation with a tractable population regression flow.
method.mechanism: A single-layer decoder receives sequences whose next-token logits sum feature-transformed weighted lag groups. Empirical full and minimal Transformers are tracked through attention maps, value-feature alignments, excess loss, and KL distance to restricted-context predictors. The theory replaces classification by population least squares, singleton groups, isotropic inputs, orthogonal feature directions, and position-only softmax attention. This yields a tensor-factorization flow. Coupled heads approach the dominant saddle; a perturbed head later leaves it, while the coupled ensemble cancels its residual cross-term, and an ordered residual-flow argument repeats for later features.
assumptions: Feature-matrix Frobenius norm is an adequate scalar definition of statistical importance.
The lag groups and feature directions can be cleanly ordered even though the original classification task is non-identifiable.
Finite-logit attention sufficiently approximates the limiting sparse patterns used in the construction and proofs.
The default synthetic Markov process with h=3, d=50, T=20, and simple grouped lags captures head interactions relevant to less controlled sequence data.
One-hot or absolute positional encodings do not introduce a qualitatively different learning mechanism from realistic relative or rotary encodings.
The regression surrogate's isotropic input covariance and mutually orthogonal feature matrices preserve the relevant geometry.
Singleton groups in the theory capture the behavior of length-two or length-four intervals in the classification experiments.
Population continuous-time gradient flow is a useful proxy for finite-sample AdamW or SGD cross-entropy training.
Near-symmetric initialization enters the ordered basin used by Theorems 1-5.
Finite-time epsilon-exp(c t) stability is long enough for the idealized phase analysis to describe actual stage transitions.
The fast-ensemble approximation behind Equation 9 is accurate around cooperative phases.
Early stopping at an intermediate stage corresponds to useful implicit regularization rather than merely undertraining.

techniques.role: Generates next tokens from several weighted lag groups paired with feature matrices of decreasing norm.
Shows that one attention head per group can copy the required positions and apply the associated feature map.
Visualizes each head's mass over lag groups through the competitive and cooperative phases.
Measures KL divergence to predictors using progressively larger prefixes of the importance-ordered groups.
Varies initialization, importance gaps, sample size, depth, optimizer, interval order, overlap, and within-group weights.
Reduces position-only softmax attention under squared loss to a tractable tensor-factorization objective.
Models the initial symmetric ensemble that converges toward the dominant position-feature saddle.
Separates one free head from the remaining ensemble and captures cancellation in their value matrices.
Proves ordering preservation, convergence in the idealized flow, and finite-time closeness to coupled systems.
Initializes simplified ODEs at observed stage boundaries and compares their trajectories with the full regression simulation.

evaluations.baseline: Random initialization and the ideal one-head-per-group sparse construction

evaluations.result: The full model passes near the I(1)-only predictor, then the I(1:2) predictor, before approaching the complete I(1:3) predictor

evaluations.baseline: Default asymmetric initialization and m>1 importance hierarchy

evaluations.metric: Best validation loss, number of observed stages, and KL to restricted-context predictors

limitations: Author-stated: the task distribution is non-identifiable; overlapping nonsparse decompositions can represent the same conditional distribution as the sparse disjoint target.
Author-stated: isotropic input covariance and orthogonal feature matrices are imposed for tractability, and general covariance geometry is outside the analysis.

Author-stated: the theory uses a population regression objective with singleton groups, while the Transformer experiments use finite-sample cross-entropy and longer intervals; their trajectory comparison is qualitative.
Author-stated: exact sparse attention is a limiting construction requiring diverging logit gaps; trained finite models only approximate it.
Author-stated: extending the account to more realistic architectures, objectives, and data distributions remains future work.

Reviewer-identified: the default experiments use h=3, d=50, one synthetic process family, and the configuration table reports seed 0; no repeated-run intervals or statistical tests establish robustness of stage timing.

Reviewer-identified: the empirical models have one or two blocks and hidden dimension 255, so the paper does not test language-model scale, natural text, long-range semantics, or learned rotary position representations.
Reviewer-identified: Theorems 2 and 3 provide closeness only for finite time proportional to negative log initialization error, not through an entire unconstrained training trajectory.
Reviewer-identified: Theorem 3 assumes the offshooting attention remains at least delta away from the dominant vertex for all time, a condition not independently established for the full system.
Reviewer-identified: Theorem 4 additionally requires ordered alignment and a positive-potential condition; Remark 2 gives one sufficient perturbation rather than proving random training enters it.
Reviewer-identified: the fast-ensemble/two-scale reduction used for cooperation is motivated by simulations rather than bounded as an approximation to the full flow.
Reviewer-identified: the low-data sample-efficiency claim is suggestive; the paper does not report a formal generalization guarantee or compare early stopping against matched explicit regularization.
Reviewer-identified: many empirical conclusions rely on attention heatmaps and KL curves without numerical tables, seed distributions, or uncertainty.

Reviewer-identified: overlapping intervals alter the selected solution, so recovery of the named sparse disjoint decomposition is an empirical implicit-bias observation rather than a general identifiability result.
Reviewer-identified: Appendix Theorem 5 appears to omit m-star-n in the limiting value matrix, creating an unresolved scale inconsistency.
Reviewer-identified: optimizer and depth ablations show qualitative persistence but do not isolate which architectural components are necessary in realistic multi-layer Transformers.
failure_modes: Perfectly symmetric head initialization can trap all heads on one pattern and prevent division of labor.
Small importance gaps can make stages merge, defeating an interpretation based on clearly separated capability jumps.
Overlapping or correlated lag groups can remove a unique importance ordering and induce alternative sparse solutions.
General input covariance can rotate or couple feature directions, invalidating the scalar norm ordering used by the proof.
A head can attend to the right group while its value matrix supplies a compensating or canceling map, making attention-only interpretation misleading.
Finite-sample noise can cause later, weaker feature directions to overfit even while early stopping retains dominant groups.
A two-scale approximation can miss feedback when the supposedly fast ensemble and offshooting head evolve on comparable timescales.
Longer or deeper models may implement the same task with distributed multi-layer circuits rather than one sparse head per group.
Finite logits can leave residual attention that produces cross-terms not captured by an ideal one-hot analysis.
A missing feature-scale factor in the arbitrary-head theorem can propagate to incorrect quantitative predictions for later stages.
reusable_insights: Track both attention and value matrices: specialization in one can require compensation in the other.
Compare a model trajectory with explicit restricted-capacity predictors to determine whether performance stages correspond to functional complexity stages.
Use exact-symmetry and equal-importance ablations to distinguish symmetry breaking from statistical ordering.
Treat intermediate plateaus as potentially useful misspecified models, then test their held-out risk rather than assuming they are merely optimization failures.
Prove a head-interaction mechanism in a surrogate only after stating which full-model quantities are preserved and which comparisons remain qualitative.
Audit task identifiability before interpreting recovered heads as the unique ground-truth decomposition.
Initialize simplified dynamical systems at empirically detected stage boundaries and compare complete trajectories, not just fixed points.
Report stage timing across seeds, data sizes, and perturbation scales because logarithmic escape times can create apparent discontinuities.
Check dimensional and magnitude consistency when extending a two-feature convergence theorem to arbitrary stages.
open_questions: Do competitive-to-cooperative head dynamics appear in natural-language training when the relevant features and lag groups are not known in advance?
Can the theory accommodate correlated tokens, nonorthogonal feature maps, and overlapping groups without assuming a scalar importance order?
What distribution over random initializations enters the basins required by Theorems 1, 4, and 5?
Can finite-time closeness bounds be extended through complete saddle-to-saddle transitions?
Is the fast-ensemble approximation provably accurate, and what controls the separation of its timescales?
Does early stopping at an intermediate context length improve test loss against ridge, dropout, weight decay, and architecture-based context restriction?
How do rotary encodings, many layers, MLPs, and many more heads change offshooting and value compensation?
Can causal activation patching verify that the observed heads implement the claimed grouped copying rather than a functionally equivalent decomposition?
Does the Theorem 5 limit require m-star-n V-star-n, and do corrected higher-stage equations match simulation quantitatively?
How stable are stage order, offshooting head identity, and transition time across seeds and stochastic minibatches?

competitive_landscape.title: The Evolution of Statistical Induction Heads: In-Context Learning Markov Chains
competitive_landscape.difference: Edelman et al. already show a uniform-to-unigram-to-bigram phase sequence when multi-layer Transformers learn in-context Markov chains. The present paper studies ordinary next-token prediction from fixed unequal lag groups and contributes a different head-level mechanism: initially redundant competition, sequential positional offshooting, and value compensation. Its novelty is therefore coordination among heads on a simpler copying task, not stage-wise Transformer learning or Markov testbeds.

competitive_landscape.title: Training Dynamics of Multi-Head Softmax Attention for In-Context Learning: Emergence, Convergence, and Optimality
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen et al. already prove multi-head softmax gradient-flow phases and task allocation for in-context multi-task linear regression. The present work differs by showing all heads first collapse onto the same statistically dominant positional pattern before they specialize and by analyzing cancellation through value matrices. It does not match the prior's broad convergence and optimality guarantee for its full 141-page model.

competitive_landscape.title: The emergence of sparse attention: impact of data distribution and benefits of repetition
competitive_landscape.difference: Zucchet et al. already analyze escape from uniform attention, power-law emergence times, data-distribution effects, and repetition benefits in a one-head sparse-attention setting. The current paper explicitly builds on essentially the same position-only data model but adds multiple interacting heads, the competitive-to-cooperative transition, sequential feature residualization, and compensatory value dynamics.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning In-context n-grams with Transformers: Sub-n-grams Are Near-stationary Points
competitive_landscape.difference: Varre et al. formalize sub-n-gram estimators as near-stationary points and connect them to discrete training stages. The current paper replaces increasing n-gram order with an importance-ordered union of positional groups and explains how symmetric heads jointly traverse the stages. Its restricted-context ladder is analogous prior structure; the new element is the within-stage multi-head interaction.

competitive_landscape.title: Unveiling Induction Heads: Provable Training Dynamics and Feature Learning in Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen et al. prove convergence of a two-layer Transformer on n-gram Markov data to a copier-selector-classifier induction circuit with relative positions and normalization. The present paper studies a shallower direct-copying primitive and provides finer temporal evidence about competition and offshooting, but its theory uses a substantially simpler regression surrogate and does not establish a complete realistic induction circuit.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Transformers acquire several sparse attention patterns incrementally without an explicit curriculum: heads first compete for the most statistically important pattern, then cooperate through sequential specialization, and simplified gradient-flow equations prove stage-wise convergence.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper provides a constructive grouped-lag task, attention and value trajectories for full and minimal one-block models, restricted-context KL probes, initialization/importance/data-size ablations, a tensor-factorization reduction, convergence and finite-time stability theorems for coupled and offshooting systems, regression simulations, and appendix variations through two blocks, overlap, online data, and SGD.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: After statistical induction-head phases, multi-head task-allocation theory, single-head sparse-attention emergence, and sub-n-gram stationary-point results, the defensible novelty is the specific competitive-to-cooperative interaction: redundant heads first learn the same dominant positional copy rule, then one offshoots while the remaining value maps cancel its residual contribution. The mathematical account is informative but conditional and surrogate-specific; it does not prove this mechanism for arbitrary initialization, finite-sample cross-entropy, realistic covariances, natural language, or large Transformers. Non-identifiability, single-run plotting, the unproved two-scale approximation, and the apparent Theorem 5 scale omission further narrow the claim.
